questions.explain: RDS automated snapshots support point-in-time recovery within the retention window of up to 35 days, and PITR on RDS restores to a new instance — restoring 'in place' is not how RDS works, so plan for the new-instance workflow including endpoint updates.
options: In-place restore to any second within 90 days
Restore to a new instance with PITR within the retention window (up to 35 days)
PITR is not supported on RDS for SQL Server
Snapshot restore that overwrites the primary
questions.q: How does point-in-time recovery work on RDS for SQL Server?

questions.explain: WITH COMPRESSION reduces storage and transfer costs, WITH CHECKSUM catches corruption at backup time rather than restore time — both belong on every native backup.
options: WITH COMPRESSION and WITH CHECKSUM on every backup
WITHOUT COMPRESSION to keep restores fast
Backups without checksums to save CPU
Compression only on full backups
questions.q: What is the native-backup discipline for compression and integrity?

questions.explain: RESTORE VERIFYONLY checks readability, not recoverability — only a real restore proves the chain. The chapter's cadence includes automated weekly restores with DBCC CHECKDB and smoke tests.
options: RESTORE VERIFYONLY proves the backup will restore
VERIFYONLY checks readability, not recoverability — only a real restore proves the chain
Checksums make restore testing unnecessary
Weekly restores are only needed for production
questions.q: What does RESTORE VERIFYONLY actually prove?

questions.explain: A 4 TB restore at 200 MB/s takes about 5.5 hours — that number belongs in the RTO document, measured now, not discovered during the outage.
options: Restore speed is always fast enough in the cloud
It should be measured during the outage
Restore throughput is the platform's responsibility
Measure restore throughput now and record it in the RTO document — e.g., 4 TB at 200 MB/s is ~5.5 hours
questions.q: Why must you measure restore throughput in advance?

questions.explain: Backups in two regions protect against regional failure; backups in a second account protect against compromised credentials — use separate-account backup vaults with write-only access from production (production can write, cannot delete).
options: Keep all backups in the production account for simplicity
Give production delete access to the backup vault
Use a second account's backup vault with write-only access from production, and alert when a scheduled copy does not complete
Cross-region copies are unnecessary for SQL Server
questions.q: What protects backups against a regional failure and against compromised credentials?

title: Chapter 29: Backup and Restore in the Cloud
